thread.title: G20 Summit: Expected To Be As Volatile As Earnings

author: Joe Albano
title: G20 Summit: Expected To Be As Volatile As Earnings
text:
I've been surprised by the lack of G20-type of articles on the front page of Seeking Alpha considering this event could be a catalyst as powerful as earnings - for the entire market! It's as if every major company will have another earnings event during the Q3 season on Sunday night.
At least that's what the market is telling me.
Why Is G20 A Catalyst? It makes sense first to understand how the G20 summit can be a catalyst of this magnitude, and then prove the market's expectations through the predicted volatility.
For those not watching the news (or those who enjoy their lives through the lack of traditional news media), the G20 summit is an annual meeting of 20 world leaders in one location to discuss international financial stability. This year's meeting in Argentina starts on Friday and ends Saturday. There will be conversations as a group as well as country to country, and it's the latter format which is in the spotlight.
You don't need to follow news media outlets to understand the importance of a China and US meeting at this economic juncture. Both China and the United States will have their presidents as representatives - head honcho to head honcho. With tariffs being imposed on China as early as January of this year and more enacted in the following months, talks with China have been a spotlight of the markets, specifically the indirect or direct result of tariffs weakening the US economy.
According to a Reuters poll , every economist surveyed said the Trump tariffs would not benefit the US economy. Now, that's a bit of a slanted survey considering tariffs are not meant to improve the economy of the country imposing them - tariffs were not designed as an economy-boosting initiative. Instead, they are used with the intent to protect domestic production. Its effectiveness aside, the markets don't like seeing a policy which hurts the economy with only a potential for at most a flat response in the other direction.
And with trade-talks stalled in the last few months combined with further action taken by the US Commerce Department against Fujian Jinhua and United Microelectronics ( UMC ), this meeting between the two world leaders has given the market a reason something will happen, especially as the two have not met since over a year ago.
Unlike the recent elections - which have polls, surveys, and models to predict a likelihood of outcomes - the meeting between these two countries has little to no basis for odds of a result. Both sides have issues they want to be resolved, with the US demanding some close-handed tenets while China doesn't appear to be the kid on the playground who likes getting pushed around. The problem for the market is there is no indicator leaning toward success (resolution) or leaning toward failure (continued course of tariffs).
Is It As Big A Deal As I'm Saying? I could very well be talking up this event and have no real basis to do so as there are some who see this event as a "figurehead-type" of a meeting, where what gets said at the dinner on Saturday night is merely political because the real negotiations and agreements happen at the lower levels of each countries' cabinets.
While that is typically how two countries work deals and manage relations, the market is still looking to the G20 event as the place in time where something will happen.
How do I know this?
First, let me explain the science of the observation. Leading up to a company's earnings, the market sets stock price expectations. These expectations get translated into options pricing for the underlying security. For example, if AMD ( AMD ) had earnings next Wednesday, then the December 7th at-the-money calls and puts are priced with the expectation of the stock movement. As AMD is rather volatile during and after earnings, options pricing usually shows an expected 8%-15% move (as one example).
A rough way to formulate this expected move is to find the expiration date of the options for the week of earnings. So using the above hypothetical timeline, you would use the December 7th expiration to make the calculation as earnings would be two days prior. Whatever week earnings are, you're looking at the end of that week's options expiration. Then you take the at-the-money strike and add the price of the call and put. So if AMD is trading for $21.45, you would find the price of the $21.50 call and the price of the $21.50 put. Today's prices for the Dec 7 expiration are $0.88 and $0.93, respectively. Adding these together you get the total expected movement of $1.81. Now to get the percentage of movement, simply divide by the strike. $1.81 divided by $21.50 multiplied by 100 gets us 8.4%
The reason for adding both is due to a common strategy in options. The idea is to play both sides of the event, this way if it goes up or goes down you are in a position to profit - this is called a straddle. The risk is if the security doesn't move enough to profit. Therefore, you're looking for at least a move of 8.4% in one direction to break-even. Anything more is profit.
By going through this exercise with actual numbers from Thursday, November 29th, you've seen the market's expectations for an 8.4% move in AMD next week. Comparatively, the Dec 14th options are priced at $1.18 and $1.21, respectively. This is only an additional $0.58, meaning Dec 14th is only expecting an additional 2.7% move week-over-week - meaning next week is expected to move three times as much as Dec 14th (roughly, as some time premium is added for the additional five days).
But we know AMD already reported earnings at the end of October, so why would the market expect such a large move for next week? There's only one major event before Dec 7th, and that's the G20 summit. The market expects some kind of market-moving rhetoric to exit the meeting and move AMD.
Could AMD have some conference or event specific to itself? Yes, but AMD's Investor Relations page says no such thing. Perhaps this is more widespread than AMD. What about other stocks or even an index like the NASDAQ ( QQQ )?
Security G20 Expected Move Dec 14th Expected Move NASDAQ ( QQQ ) 3.3% 0.44% Micron ( MU ) 6.2% 1.6% Facebook ( FB ) 4.2% 1.6% Cummins ( CMI ) 3.6% 1.2% Apple ( AAPL ) 4.1% 1.1% Paypal ( PYPL ) 4.1% 1.3% Netflix ( NFLX ) 6.9% 2.1% (Source: Options data from TD Ameritrade)
These are earnings-type of moves for most of the stocks mentioned. It's clear there is a volatile move being priced in. Some may even say it's a little conservative. For the NASDAQ, this is quite drastic as depicted by the blue arrow range of where 3.3% can take the index in just a few days. Remember, this is just what is expected, not necessarily what will happen. There are many times options predictions are under or over. The idea here is to show the market expects more volatility than a usual week.
Herein lies your choices (I would say options but that's just too ... easy?): escape the volatility and move to cash, continue holding a long portfolio and hope for some kind of positive outcome to the Summit, short the market and look for the talk to fail, or play the straddle looking for a move beyond what the options market is pricing.
Personally, I'm planning to take the less risky approach by continuing to hold my shares so as not to miss any upside but leave dry powder available to buy if the market takes a hit. The downside to looking to buy on a drop is it may not be the bottom but rather the continuation of a slide started back in October as more tariffs may be on the way - a setup the market already doesn't like.
In any case, I want you to be aware of the potential volatility coming from this weekend's meeting between China and the US. A positive outcome could be the beginning of a rally while a negative outcome and more of the same tension could be the acceleration of a deeper rut for the market.
